answer: The CIA records describe a source’s account of a sighting at Site 7, Sary Shagan, on an evening in late summer 1973. The source said they saw a bright green circular object or mass in the sky west of the site. Within 10–15 seconds, it widened and several green concentric circles formed around it. The color faded within minutes, and the source heard no sound. The source could not determine its altitude or size; the fragments record no explanation for it [UNDATED-CIA-6E72CA] [UNDATED-CIA-158652].

The archive contains two records concerning Chief Petty Officer Delbert C. Newhouse’s July 2, 1952, sighting about seven miles north of Tremonton, Utah. One says he used a hand-held 16mm color camera to film approximately 30 feet of footage showing 10–12 unidentified objects milling about in rough formation and moving west. It says one object reversed course and was tracked separately across the camera’s field of view several times. That fragment records the case as unresolved [1952-USN-80203D].

A separate record describes the same witness, time, and vicinity, but says two photographs were taken and that the objects appeared too small on film to show detail. Its fragment is marked “identified,” without an explanation in the supplied evidence of what the objects were. The records have separate canonical-event entries, so the evidence does not establish whether they document distinct occurrences or differing accounts of the same sighting [1952-DOW-141453] [1952-USN-80203D].
The December 12, 1948 green fireball was reported in New Mexico, near Starvation Peak (Bernal) and Los Alamos. The archive says it was observed from two stations there. [1948-USAF-DDD5CA]

On 19 November 1968, USS Clyatt’s radar detected an unidentified object near Puerto Rico. The record says it appeared on radar for about 21 seconds and seemed to close on a fighter from the east to within a few miles. Its identity remained unresolved [1968-USN-6F2707].

The Colorado Springs 2022 narrative described a potato-shaped object with distinct edges and a creamy-white, opalescent appearance over the Cheyenne Mountains. The witnesses reported that it stayed still for about two minutes before vanishing [UNDATED-USA-599D8B].
The witness reported that the lights formed a triangular pattern with a light in the center. This describes the arrangement of the lights, not a confirmed triangular object [UNDATED-FBI-380101].

The archive describes the “ghost rockets” as a **1946 series of reports across Scandinavia**, not a single sighting. Press reports began in southern Sweden in late May; reports followed from Finland and Denmark in June and Norway by July. Swedish authorities received nearly 1,000 reports through October. Witnesses described objects as “a ball of fire with a tail” or “shiny cigar-shaped objects” [UNDATED-DOW-EA3896].

A separate archive account describes sightings in Swedish skies from February to December 1946, generally of elongated objects, sometimes resembling spheres or disks. Some reportedly left luminous trails or appeared to ascend or descend suddenly. That account says the sightings concerned military authorities in several countries [1946-NASA-A146CF].

The supplied fragments do not give a consistent resolution: the general-campaign fragment is marked *identified*, while the Swedish-sightings fragment is marked *unresolved*. Neither supplied excerpt explains an identification, so the evidence does not establish what the reported objects were [UNDATED-DOW-EA3896] [1946-NASA-A146CF].

On the night of 19 November, the Crusader pilot reported seeing a delta-shaped object about the size of a jet fighter near Puerto Rico. He observed it in full moonlight, with good weather and visibility. The archive summary says its estimated speed exceeded Mach 3; the supplied excerpt does not say how that speed was estimated. The fragment records the sighting as unresolved. [1968-USN-85858D]

On October 4, 1955, a U.S. tourist and three companions aboard a train approximately 50–65 miles south of Baku reported seeing a squat, equilateral-triangle-shaped object on an airfield about two miles away. The witness estimated it was roughly the size of a U.S. jet fighter and described a light at each corner. A searchlight illuminated it; the witnesses said it then launched, made between three and seven rapid spirals, and climbed steeply at about a 45-degree angle while the searchlight tracked it. The fragment records the case as unresolved [1955-CIA-E34C6D].

The CIA material reports an unidentified object hovering at high altitude over Harare International Airport on the afternoon of July 2, 2008. The excerpt says it was observed “possibly by both radar and optical means.” The archive summary describes it as disc-like, with rotating lights underneath; it reportedly shifted colors and then ascended out of visual range. The fragment records the incident as unresolved [2008-CIA-052DE8].

The January 30, 1949 record describes a green fireball in the Socorro, New Mexico area. Air and ground searches in early February followed what the record called its “well determined” ground track, but recovered no fragments. The fragment’s resolution is listed as unresolved [1949-USAF-5C0132].

The archive contains an FBI report dated October 1, 2023, about a sighting near Colorado Springs. A witness said a dark-gray cloud dissipated as a large, solid black triangular object emerged, with a red light at each corner. The witness described it as initially moving at about helicopter speed, then possibly accelerating to Mach 1–2, banking unusually, and disappearing. The report is recorded as unresolved; those speeds and maneuvers are the witness’s account, not a confirmed assessment [2023-FBI-6A299C].

The Blue Book material reports a **seven-inch ball of flame with an eight-foot trail** sighted from Phoenix at about 4:20 a.m. on July 2, 1952. It was reported to travel in an arc from northwest to southwest for roughly three to four minutes; the record lists the sighting as unresolved. [1952-USAF-0585D4]

On 24 November 1968, the Atlantic Fleet Weapons Range tracked a high-speed, high-altitude target near Puerto Rico. The record says it rapidly pulled away from a Crusader aircraft flying at Mach 0.99 at 45,000 feet. The target’s identity was not resolved [1968-USN-9E57C2].

The undated New Jersey record says pilots in a T-33 chased something near Sandy Hook and Fort Monmouth. Its summary describes the object as large and disc-shaped. About ten minutes later, according to the quoted account, radar stations in the area began picking up objects moving back and forth across the sky; the summary reports speeds of up to 3,500 mph [UNDATED-USAF-58C451].

The supplied fragment labels the case “identified,” but does not say what the object was identified as. It does not establish that the pilots’ sighting and the later radar returns were the same object [UNDATED-USAF-58C451].
The agency or branch is recorded as “not stated” on both supplied Sary Shagan fragments [UNDATED-CIA-6E72CA] [UNDATED-CIA-158652].
The USS Clyatt radar case is dated 1968 [1968-USN-6F2707].
The Tremonton filming fragment records the branch as USN (U.S. Navy) [1952-USN-80203D].
The Phoenix ball-of-flame fragment is recorded as unresolved [1952-USAF-0585D4].
The Baku triangular-object fragment records the location as between the train and the Caspian Sea coast in the Azerbaijan SSR, approximately 50–65 miles south of Baku [1955-CIA-E34C6D].
The recorded location text is “Cheyenne Mountains” [UNDATED-USA-599D8B].
The December 20, 1948 Los Alamos green fireball fragment records the branch as USAF [1948-USAF-BFA2CC].
The Atlantic Fleet high-speed target fragment records the date as November 24, 1968 [1968-USN-9E57C2].
The ghost-rockets fragment records the location as southern Sweden, Finland, Denmark, and Norway [UNDATED-DOW-EA3896].
Yes. The October 2023 Colorado Springs triangular report lists “FBI” as its agency or branch in the fragment metadata [2023-FBI-6A299C].

The Western U.S. 2023 series represents **21 separate canonical events**, not one event. The listed case IDs are fragments associated with the series, so counting them would overstate the number of events [UNDATED-FBI-FEDFE7] [UNDATED-FBI-2EAE94].

The archive links three source files to the Colorado Springs 2022 event: FBI-UAP-D002.pdf as the primary narrative, FBI-UAP-D003.pdf as media for the event, and ICA-UAP-D001.pdf as analysis of the event. The supplied evidence does not describe what the media or analysis contains. These sources are associated with one canonical event, represented here by a single observation fragment [UNDATED-USA-599D8B].

No. The archive lists the Colorado Springs media rendering as *media for* the Cheyenne Mountain observation, within the same canonical event—not as a separate incident [UNDATED-USA-599D8B]. The October 2023 black-triangle report is listed as a different Colorado Springs event [2023-FBI-6A299C].

The supplied archive evidence identifies ICA-UAP-D001.pdf as an analysis source for the Colorado Springs 2022 event, but it does not provide that analysis’s findings or methods. The incident fragment describes an observation over Cheyenne Mountain and records it as unresolved. On this evidence, there is no basis to say what the analysis concluded [UNDATED-USA-599D8B].

The two Sary Shagan fragments describe the same place: Site 7 at Sary Shagan. Both report a late-summer 1973 observation of a bright green circular object west of the site. They are listed under separate canonical-event entries, so the supplied evidence does not establish whether they represent one event or two; it does not describe unrelated countries. [UNDATED-CIA-6E72CA] [UNDATED-CIA-158652]

The Tremonton material should be described as **one filming episode**, not several unrelated events. The supplied archive places the fragment under one canonical event: Newhouse’s filming on July 2, 1952, near Tremonton. His footage reportedly showed a group of objects, with one object then tracked separately; that change in what he filmed does not make it a separate event [1952-USN-80203D].

The three November 1968 records all concern unresolved U.S. Navy reports near Puerto Rico involving unidentified objects and Crusader fighters. On 19 November, USS Clyatt briefly detected an object on radar closing on a fighter, while a Crusader pilot reported seeing a delta-shaped object that night. On 24 November, the Atlantic Fleet Weapons Range tracked a high-speed, high-altitude target pulling away from another Crusader. The archive lists these as three distinct canonical events, not one confirmed encounter. [1968-USN-6F2707] [1968-USN-85858D] [1968-USN-9E57C2]

No. The supplied records describe the December 12 and December 20, 1948 Los Alamos-area green fireballs as separate observations, and both fragments are marked unresolved—not identified as an aircraft [1948-USAF-DDD5CA] [1948-USAF-BFA2CC]. The undated New Mexico report also describes multiple green-fireball reports without identifying them as an aircraft [UNDATED-USAF-B32231].

It describes a series of events, not one object seen once. The archive groups 21 separate canonical events under the Western US Event series. The supplied accounts include a road encounter involving a vehicle-like object with red and white lights, a report of a dark kite-shaped object, and orange-orb sightings reported at least five times over two days [UNDATED-FBI-63F44E] [UNDATED-FBI-B8A3AB] [UNDATED-OTHER-26A05E]. These are reported observations, not a determination that every sighting involved the same object.

The **2022 Cheyenne Mountain narrative** is the undated Army fragment associated with the canonical “Colorado Springs 2022” event. It describes a former Army intelligence officer and four unit members reportedly seeing a creamy-white, potato-shaped object over Cheyenne Mountain that remained still for about two minutes before vanishing. FBI-UAP-D002.pdf is its primary narrative; FBI-UAP-D003.pdf is listed as media for the same event, not a separate incident [UNDATED-USA-599D8B].

The **October 2023 triangular report** is a separate Colorado Springs event, dated October 1, 2023. Its witness described a black triangular object with red lights at its corners emerging from a dissipating cloud, then accelerating and banking before disappearing. FBI-UAP-D030.pdf is its primary narrative [2023-FBI-6A299C].

Both fragments are marked unresolved; the supplied evidence does not establish an explanation for either observation [UNDATED-USA-599D8B] [2023-FBI-6A299C].

The supplied Tremonton records leave the identification uncertain. One fragment records Newhouse filming objects he and his wife could not identify and labels the case unresolved; another fragment for the same date and area is labeled identified, but the supplied text does not say what the objects were identified as or explain the differing labels [1952-USN-80203D] [1952-DOW-141453]. The evidence therefore does not establish a clear official explanation for what was filmed.

Yes. The Crusader pilot’s observation and the USS Clyatt radar detection were both reported on 19 November 1968 in the vicinity of Puerto Rico [1968-USN-85858D] [1968-USN-6F2707]. The archive lists them as separate canonical events, so the supplied evidence does not establish that the pilot and radar observed the same object. A separate Crusader-related range report is dated 24 November, also in that Puerto Rico window [1968-USN-9E57C2].

For the Cheyenne Mountain observation grouped under the Colorado Springs 2022 event, FBI-UAP-D002.pdf is the primary narrative and FBI-UAP-D003.pdf is the media file for that same event [UNDATED-USA-599D8B]. The evidence identifies their relationship but does not describe what the media file contains.

No. The 1948 records name Los Alamos for the December 20 sighting [1948-USAF-BFA2CC], and both near Starvation Peak (Bernal) and Los Alamos, New Mexico, for the December 12 sighting, which was observed from two stations [1948-USAF-DDD5CA].

No. The archive identifies the October 2023 Colorado law-enforcement video and the Cheyenne Mountain narrative as different fragments in different canonical events. The video is a 1-minute, 19-second recording captured by a Colorado law-enforcement officer [UNDATED-LLE-A4576B]. The Cheyenne Mountain fragment describes an Army intelligence officer and four unit members observing an object over Cheyenne Mountain; its canonical event is labeled “Colorado Springs 2022” [UNDATED-USA-599D8B].

The files describe a cluster of reported green or greenish-blue fireballs, but they do not give them all the same explanation. A USAF account of reports around New Mexico, Los Alamos, and Albuquerque says the objects were described as meteor-like, with apparently flat trajectories and no explosion; that account leaves them unresolved [UNDATED-USAF-B32231].

The dated 1949 records report a January 30 green fireball in the Socorro area. Air and ground searches along its estimated ground track recovered no fragments [1949-USAF-5C0132]. A separate record says a bright green fireball was reported near Socorro at 8:26 p.m. on July 24, 1949, and that airborne material was collected in an attempt to find associated particles; the supplied evidence gives no result from that collection [1949-USAF-9D1046]. Another account describes a January 30 fireball over Texas as exceptionally bright, based on comparisons with the moon rather than the speaker’s own observation. The supplied records do not establish that it was the same sighting as the January 30 Socorro report [UNDATED-DOE-5FC004].

The undated discussions add observations but should not be assigned a late-1940s date on this evidence alone. They contrast a green fireball’s horizontal path with Geminid meteors and describe a separate, very bright fireball appearing from the Geminid direction roughly an hour to an hour and a half later [UNDATED-DOE-80EBE8] [UNDATED-DOE-BBFEBB]. In another report, observers at Kirtland Field and in Arizona gave different colors—bronze and green—for what the account presents as an object seen at matching times [UNDATED-USAF-6A96A7].

Not every green observation was assessed as unusual: a separately recorded, doubly observed yellow-green fireball was judged to be an ordinary fireball on the basis of its estimated heights [UNDATED-DOE-DA531C]. Overall, the supplied files preserve varied observations, unsuccessful fragment searches in one dated case, and differing assessments—not a single established explanation for all the reports.

The supplied archive evidence contains two Tremonton records, but neither is explicitly labeled as Project Blue Book material.

One record describes Chief Petty Officer Delbert C. Newhouse filming roughly 30 feet of 16mm color film on July 2, 1952, seven miles north of Tremonton. It reports about 10–12 objects moving in rough formation and says one reversed course and was filmed separately. That fragment is marked unresolved [1952-USN-80203D].

A separate record from the same date and area describes Newhouse seeing objects milling in rough formation. Its summary says two photographs were taken but the objects were too small on film to show detail; that fragment is marked identified. The supplied evidence does not explain that identification or reconcile it with the unresolved designation of the film record [1952-DOW-141453].

The supplied archive evidence lists three U.S. Navy records from November 1968 in the vicinity of Puerto Rico. Each is listed as a separate canonical event, and each fragment’s resolution is recorded as unresolved:

- On November 19, USS Clyatt detected an unidentified radar object for about 21 seconds; the account says it closed on a fighter from the east to within a few miles [1968-USN-6F2707].
- Also on November 19, a Crusader pilot reported seeing a delta-shaped object about the size of a jet fighter in good visibility. The record estimates its speed at over Mach 3 [1968-USN-85858D].
- On November 24, the Atlantic Fleet Weapons Range tracked a high-speed, high-altitude target that reportedly pulled rapidly away from a Crusader flying at Mach 0.99 and 45,000 feet [1968-USN-9E57C2].

These are reported observations and tracking accounts, not established identifications.

The supplied FBI-file evidence does not mention Newark or describe a sighting there. It describes reports from other New Jersey locations, including Glen Ridge, Union, Perth Amboy, Woodbridge, and West Orange [1957-FBI-DB9934] [1958-FBI-B518F9] [1958-FBI-8A9CE1] [1958-FBI-420E8E] [1958-FBI-D3842E]. On this evidence, the archive does not say what happened in Newark.

The 1952 Utah film case represented is the Tremonton filming. On July 2, Chief Petty Officer Delbert C. Newhouse used a handheld 16mm camera to film a group of roughly 10–12 objects seven miles north of Tremonton, Utah. The record says the objects milled about in rough formation, and one was filmed separately after reversing course. That film fragment is marked unresolved [1952-USN-80203D]. A separate Tremonton fragment describes Newhouse’s observation and is marked identified, but the supplied evidence does not explain that assessment [1952-DOW-141453].

The supplied records point to four radar-related cases:

- At St. Louis, an account of a B-29 radar-bomb-scoring run says an operator saw a return at about 48,000 feet that appeared to descend toward the aircraft. The operator initially considered an equipment effect, such as “double harmonics”; the fragment records no resolution [UNDATED-USAF-5C92A2].
- In the undated New Spain Library account, a ground-controlled-approach radar operator reported two returns apparently on a collision course with an incoming C-47. The account says the returns turned just after the tower broadcast a warning; it remains unresolved in the supplied fragment [UNDATED-USAF-539CFA].
- A pilot near Japan reported tracking multiple objects on a radar/sensor screen, with three visible at once at one point. The fragment records the case as unresolved [2020-USAF-82CB61].
- A January 28, 1994, track was reportedly detected and recorded on radar at the Cinq-Mars-la-Pile Control and Detection Center in France. The supplied fragment records no identification [1994-USAF-3880AD].

These are reported observations in the supplied files, not established explanations of what produced the returns.

The supplied archive evidence includes several green-fireball records connected to Los Alamos and New Mexico, plus one item from a DOE-labeled source file. The listed Los Alamos-area cases are classified here as USAF records, not as Department of Energy incidents.

Two December 1948 reports describe distinct observations: a greenish-yellow fireball seen from two New Mexico stations near Starvation Peak and Los Alamos, with an estimated nearly horizontal path [1948-USAF-DDD5CA]; and a greenish-white fireball observed by Los Alamos AESS inspectors that reportedly descended and then followed a nearly horizontal path [1948-USAF-BFA2CC]. An undated account discusses reports of greenish-blue fireballs near Los Alamos and Albuquerque, described as having flat trajectories and not exploding [UNDATED-USAF-B32231].

The evidence also lists two Socorro-area green-fireball reports. Airborne material was collected in an attempt to find particles associated with the July 24, 1949 report [1949-USAF-9D1046]. Air and ground searches found no fragments from the January 30, 1949 fireball [1949-USAF-5C0132].

The DOE-labeled source file contains a separate, undated report of an August 4 green fireball near Oregon; its excerpt notes the timing’s proximity to a meteor shower [UNDATED-DOE-A60A48]. All of these fragments are marked unresolved in the supplied evidence.

The archive contains transcripts associated with two videos recorded by Colorado law-enforcement officers in October 2023:

- A 1-minute, 19-second recording, titled LLE-UAP-PR 00J in the collection. AARO removed its audio to protect privacy and sensitive information. The fragment records the UAP as unresolved. [UNDATED-LLE-A4576B]
- A 27-second recording, titled LLE-UAP-PR003. Its audio contained indistinct background noise but no discernible dialogue; this fragment also records the UAP as unresolved. [UNDATED-LLE-2234ED]

The supplied evidence does not describe what appears in either video or identify the officers’ agencies.

The archive includes a CIA source file, CIA-UAP-011.pdf, describing a sighting at Site 7 of the Sary Shagan weapons testing range in late summer 1973. A Soviet citizen reported seeing a bright green circular object west of the site; it expanded into concentric circles and faded without a sound. The fragment records the sighting as unresolved and does not give the report itself a date [UNDATED-CIA-158652].

The released material describes a 1946 Scandinavian reporting wave, not one single ghost-rocket incident. One account says the press first reported “flying missiles” over southern Sweden in late May and named them “Ghost Rockets.” Reports extended to Finland and Denmark in June and Norway by July; Swedish authorities reportedly received nearly 1,000 reports through October. Descriptions included a “ball of fire with a tail” and shiny cigar-shaped objects [UNDATED-DOW-EA3896].

A separate account gives a broader February–December 1946 span. It describes objects in Swedish skies as generally fusiform, occasionally sphere- or disk-shaped, usually moving horizontally, sometimes leaving luminous trails, and reportedly capable of sudden ascent or descent. It says the sightings concerned military authorities in several countries [1946-NASA-A146CF].

The supplied evidence does not establish that these differently framed accounts describe identical sightings. It also gives no explanation for the objects: one fragment is marked “identified,” but the supplied text does not say *as what*, while the other is marked “unresolved” [UNDATED-DOW-EA3896] [1946-NASA-A146CF].

No. These records describe observations that were unresolved or had insufficient data; they do not establish that extraterrestrials visited Earth. For example, a search after the 1949 New Mexico fireball recovered no fragments, and the Sandia Base light observation is marked as having insufficient data [1949-USAF-5C0132] [1949-USA-E98687]. The Mexican Congress record reports testimony and the presentation of *alleged* alien corpses—not a verified finding of extraterrestrial origin [2023-DEPARTMENT-98C959].

The supplied archive evidence describes no alien species. It contains reports of unidentified objects and lights, but no descriptions of beings or official identification of an extraterrestrial species—for example, the Cheyenne Mountain account describes an object, not its occupants [UNDATED-USA-599D8B].

None of the supplied archive evidence establishes that any UAP definitely used anti-gravity. The records describe observations—including a steep climb near Baku [1955-CIA-E34C6D] and a target rapidly pulling away from an aircraft near Puerto Rico [1968-USN-9E57C2]—but do not identify anti-gravity as the cause.

None of the supplied government records proves that alien bodies were recovered. The closest is an FBI record of an auto dealer relaying engineer Coulter’s claim that he saw recovered “flying saucers” and non-human remains. The archive records that as an unresolved, secondhand claim—not a verified recovery [UNDATED-FBI-AC2C].

The supplied archive evidence does not identify a pilot for any of the observed objects. In the Gemini 5 account, Cooper and Conrad were the astronauts aboard the spacecraft from which the object was observed, but the record does not say which of them was piloting it [UNDATED-USN-35D21A].

None of the supplied cases conclusively proves non-human technology. The recovery accounts are presented as claims, including Coulter’s reported sighting of recovered saucers [UNDATED-FBI-AC2C] and the account attributed to Colonel Corso about Roswell [1947-USAF-A120D8]. Both fragments are recorded as unresolved; neither establishes that the claimed technology was non-human.

The supplied archive evidence does not identify or substantiate a secret treaty with an alien government. One FBI record recounts a secondhand claim about recovered “flying saucers,” but it mentions no treaty [UNDATED-FBI-AC2C]. A record of testimony before the Mexican Congress describes a proposed law, not an agreement with an alien government [2023-DEPARTMENT-98C959].

None of the supplied files confirms a weaponized UFO. One witness described an unidentified object as *resembling* an underwater demolition bomb, but the record does not say it was a weapon [1957-USAF-861A2D]. Another witness described an object as “bullet-shaped”; that describes its appearance, not its function [1958-FBI-B518F9].

The supplied records do not locate or name an extraterrestrial base. “Sandia Base” and “Killeen Base” are named as locations of reported observations, not as extraterrestrial bases [1949-USA-E98687] [1949-USA-DEB3F3].

None of the supplied records proves a crash retrieval of a flying saucer. The Roswell fragment says the base initially announced recovery of debris from a “flying disk,” then retracted that account and called it a weather balloon [1947-USAF-2C9F14]. A separate FBI fragment records Coulter’s claim that he saw two recovered saucers, but it does not verify the claim [UNDATED-FBI-AC2C].
